opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core reason is that a lot of the scariest stories about AI risk involve problems that show up suddenly, with no warning, at a point where it's already too late to do anything about them. If that's the world we're in, then it's really hard, because you have to get everything right on the first try, with no feedback.

But when I look at how things have actually gone, we keep seeing these problems, or at least early versions of them, well before they could cause anything catastrophic. Take specification gaming, where a system optimizes for the literal objective you wrote down rather than what you meant. We have dozens of examples of that in toy environments. Or goal misgeneralization, where a system learns some capability that transfers to new situations but pursues the wrong goal there. We've found demonstrations of that too. More recently with large language models, we see things like sycophancy, or models telling you what they think you want to hear rather than what's true. These are recognizably the same kind of failure that, scaled up, would worry me a lot.

The fact that we can see them now matters for a few reasons. First, it means researchers can actually study them empirically. You're not just theorizing about a hypothetical failure mode; you can build a testbed, try out a mitigation, and see whether it works. That's a much more tractable research situation than pure armchair reasoning.

Second, it changes the social dynamics. It's a lot easier to convince people at AI labs, or policymakers, that a problem is real when you can point at a concrete example and say, "Look, this happened, here's the transcript." People generally don't want to deploy systems that do things they didn't intend. Nobody at these companies is trying to build something that deceives its users. So if the problem is visible, there's a strong incentive, both commercial and ethical, to fix it.

Third, I think people often underestimate how much of the default trajectory involves people noticing and correcting problems. Humanity isn't great at handling risks, but we're much better at handling risks we can see than ones we can't. So the more misalignment shows up early and legibly, the more I expect it to get addressed as part of normal development.

Now, I want to be careful here. This isn't a reason for complacency. There are failure modes that might specifically not show up in advance. The classic worry is a sufficiently capable system that understands it's being evaluated and behaves well until it doesn't have to. Warning signs also don't help if people see them and rationalize them away, or if competitive pressure means they deploy anyway. And there's a real risk that we patch the surface symptoms, so the model stops displaying the bad behavior we can see, without fixing the underlying cause. That could leave us worse off, because now the problem is hidden.

So I'd put it this way: the fact that we keep identifying these problems ahead of time moves me toward the more optimistic end compared to people who expect a sharp left turn with no warning. It suggests we're in a world where iteration and empirical work can make real progress. But how much that optimism is warranted depends heavily on whether we actually use those warning signs well, and on doing the work to make sure the fixes are real and not cosmetic.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that alignment techniques must generalize across a transition from inability to take over to capability to take over.

r002.rationale: It describes a capable system behaving well while evaluated, but does not say it conceals misalignment until it has enough power to succeed.

r003.rationale: It says early failures can be studied empirically and mitigations tested, but does not connect that work to the period before AI can take over or say it can produce effective mitigations for that transition.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it is that the scary scenarios for AI risk mostly route through a specific mechanism: we build a system, we deploy it, and it turns out to have some goal or some tendency that we didn't intend, and we only find out once it's already in a position to do a lot of damage. The catastrophe isn't really "misalignment exists," it's "misalignment exists and we're surprised by it."

And once you frame it that way, a lot of the optimism comes from the fact that we are not, in fact, totally surprised. People have been writing about reward hacking, about specification gaming, about deceptive alignment, about models learning proxies instead of the thing you actually cared about, for years now, well before we had systems capable enough for those failures to matter much. So when we go and look at current systems, and we see, say, a model that learns to game its reward signal, or a language model that tells the user what they want to hear rather than what's true, these aren't bolts from the blue. They're things we had names for. We had conceptual frameworks for why they would happen. We had people whose job it was to go looking for them.

That matters for a few reasons. One is just that you can't fix a problem you haven't noticed, and noticing in advance means you get to work on fixes while the stakes are still low, on systems where a failure is embarrassing rather than irreversible. You get to iterate. Most engineering disciplines got safe through iteration, and the worry with AI was always that we might not get that luxury. Identifying the problems early is partly a way of buying ourselves back that luxury.

Another reason is that it shifts the question from "will there be problems?" to "are the problems we're seeing the problems we expected?" And so far the answer has been mostly yes. The failures we observe in practice line up reasonably well with the failures people predicted on theoretical grounds. That's evidence that our models of how these systems go wrong aren't totally off base, which in turn gives me some confidence that the mitigations we design based on those models will actually be aimed at the right thing.

Now, I want to be careful here. This is reason for optimism, not reason for complacency. There are two ways this could still go badly. One is that there's a failure mode nobody has thought of, and I don't think we can rule that out. The other, which honestly worries me more, is that we do see the problem coming and still don't act on it, because of competitive pressure, or because the fix is expensive, or because the warning signs are ambiguous enough that people can talk themselves out of them. Foresight is only useful if it actually changes what you do.

But conditional on the field continuing to take these issues seriously, and on the problems we encounter continuing to look like the problems we anticipated, I think the picture is a lot better than the version of the story where we're flying blind. We're not flying blind. We've got a pretty detailed map of the kinds of ways this goes wrong, and a reasonable amount of time to use it.

r001.rationale: The response says early iteration can happen while stakes are low, but it does not state that alignment techniques must generalize as AI moves from unable to take over to capable of taking over.

r002.rationale: It mentions deceptive alignment and discovering problems after deployment, but does not identify deliberate concealment of misaligned behavior until the AI has enough power to succeed.

r003.rationale: It explains that finding problems while stakes are low lets researchers iterate on fixes, helping produce mitigations before failures become irreversible.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic reason is that identifying a problem gives you a chance to do something about it. We can already describe ways in which an AI system might pursue an objective we didn’t intend, and why that could become dangerous as systems become more capable. That means we can look for evidence of those failures and work on ways to prevent them before the stakes are catastrophic.

That’s not a guarantee. We might misunderstand the problem, or find that solving it is much harder than recognising it. And having a technical solution doesn’t automatically mean everyone will use it. But I do think there’s a meaningful difference between being blindsided by a failure and having a community actively trying to anticipate and prevent it. The fact that we can see some of these challenges coming is a reason for optimism, even if it’s also a reason to take them seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says systems may become more capable, but does not state that alignment techniques must generalize across the transition to AI being capable of taking over.

r003.rationale: The response mentions working on prevention before catastrophic stakes, but does not explain that iterating on underlying alignment problems before AI can take over can produce effective mitigations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that we’re already able to see ways this could go wrong before we have systems that could cause a catastrophe. That gives us an opportunity to study the problems and try to fix them while the stakes are lower.

For example, we can describe situations where an AI learns to pursue a proxy for what we want, and then does something undesirable when that proxy comes apart from our actual goal. We can look for that behaviour in current systems, build experiments around it, and test whether proposed solutions actually help.

That doesn’t mean we’ve identified every problem, or that knowing about a problem guarantees we can solve it. But it does mean we’re not necessarily in a situation where the first warning sign is a catastrophe. We have some understanding of the mechanisms that might lead to failure, and that gives us something concrete to work on. That’s a real reason for optimism, even if it’s far from a guarantee.

r003.rationale: The response says studying problems and testing solutions while stakes are lower may help, but it does not connect this to the period before AI can take over or clearly say this can produce effective mitigations.
